claim: SOX2 is the first marker of pluripotency in the mouse early embryo, expressed specifically in inside cells at the 16 cell stage
source: In contrast to other markers of pluripotency, Sox2 is expressed specifically in inside cells at the 16 cell stage, and is therefore the first marker of pluripotency in the embryo (Guo et al., 2010; Wicklow et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guo et al., 2010 and Wicklow et al., 2014

claim: CDX2 is expressed specifically in outer cells of the 16 cell embryo
source: Thus, the first cell fate decision has been studied mainly from the perspective of trophectoderm specification because the transcription factor CDX2, which is essential for trophectoderm development (Strumpf et al., 2005), is expressed specifically in outer cells of the 16 cell embryo (Ralston and Rossant, 2008), and has provided a way to distinguish future trophectoderm cells from non-trophectoderm cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to Strumpf et al., 2005 and Ralston and Rossant, 2008

claim: Sox2 is restricted to inside cells by a Cdx2-independent mechanism
source: We previously showed that Sox2 is restricted to inside cells by a Cdx2-independent mechanism (Wicklow et al., 2014), which differs from Oct4 and Nanog, which are restricted to the inner cell mass by CDX2 (Niwa et al., 2005; Strumpf et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wicklow et al., 2014, Niwa et al., 2005, and Strumpf et al., 2005

claim: HIPPO pathway kinases LATS1/2 become active in unpolarized cells located deep inside the embryo
source: In particular, the HIPPO pathway kinases LATS1/2 become active in unpolarized cells located deep inside the embryo, where they antagonize activity of the YAP1/WWTR1/TEAD4 transcriptional complex that is thought to promote expression of Cdx2 (Anani et al., 2014; Cockburn et al., 2013; Hirate et al., 2013; Kono et al., 2014; Korotkevich et al., 2017; Leung and Zernicka-Goetz, 2013; Lorthongpanich et al., 2013; Mihajlović and Bruce, 2016; Nishioka et al., 2009; Nishioka et al., 2008; Posfai et al., 2017; Rayon et al., 2014; Watanabe et al., 2017; Yagi et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: ROCK inhibitor treatment leads to reduced Cdx2 expression in embryos
source: Rho-associated, coiled-coil containing protein kinases (ROCK1 and 2) are thought to act upstream of Cdx2 because embryos developing in the presence of a ROCK-inhibitor (Y-27632, ROCKi) exhibit reduced Cdx2 expression (Kono et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kono et al., 2014

claim: Embryos cultured in ROCKi exhibit ectopic SOX2 expression in cells located on the outer surface of the embryo
source: Interestingly, in ROCKi-treated embryos, we observed ectopic SOX2 expression in cells located on the outer surface of the embryo (Figure 1C', D), indicating that ROCK1/2 participates in repressing expression of Sox2 in the trophectoderm.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C' and D

claim: ROCK inhibition leads to an increase in outside cells of mixed lineage that coexpress CDX2 and SOX2
source: However, among outside cells, a substantial proportion coexpressed CDX2 and SOX2 in ROCKi-treated embryos compared with controls (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that ROCK inhibition leads to an increase in outside cells of mixed lineage.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Nuclear YAP1 is sufficient to repress Sox2 expression in the inner cell mass
source: We observed a conspicuous decrease in the proportion of Yap1CA-overexpressing inside cells expressing detectable SOX2 (Figure 1G,H). Therefore, nuclear YAP1 is sufficient to repress Sox2 expression in the inner cell mass, indicative of a likely role for YAP1 in repressing expression of Sox2 in the trophectoderm downstream of ROCK1/2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H

claim: Almost all Lats2-overexpressing cells ended up within the inner cell mass by the blastocyst stage
source: Surprisingly, we observed that almost all Lats2-overexpressing cells ended up within the inner cell mass by the blastocyst stage (Figure 2B,C), in contrast to cells injected with GFP mRNA only, which contributed to both inner cell mass and trophectoderm.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and C

claim: SOX2 was detected in all Lats2-overexpressing cells observed within the inner cell mass
source: Notably, SOX2 was detected in all Lats2-overexpressing cells observed within the inner cell mass (Figure 2D), suggesting that Lats2-overexpressing cells were not only localized to the inner cell mass but also exhibited position-appropriate regulation of Sox2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: LATS2 is sufficient to induce expression of SOX2 in cells regardless of their position within the embryo
source: In addition to detecting SOX2 in all Lats2-overexpressing cells located inside the embryo, SOX2 was also detected in rare Lats2-overexpressing cells that remained on the embryo surface (Figure 2D). Therefore, LATS2 is sufficient to induce expression of SOX2 in cells regardless of their position within the embryo.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: LATS2 promotes inside cell positioning by regulating the activities of YAP1 and WWTR1
source: Consistent with this prediction, cooverexpression of Lats2 and Yap1CA led to a significant decrease in the proportion of Lats2-overexpressing cells contributing to the inside cell position, and a concomitant increase in the proportion of Lats2-overexpressing cells remaining in the outside position (Figure Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D). Moreover, cooverexpression of Lats2 and Yap1CA reduced the number of TUNEL positive nuclei, consistent with Yap1CA rescuing survival of outside-positioned Lats2-overexpressing cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D). Collectively, these observations strongly suggest that LATS2 promotes inside cell positioning by regulating the activities of YAP1 and, likely, the related protein WWTR1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D

claim: Lats2-overexpressing cells become underrepresented in the inside population starting around the 32-cell stage
source: Surprisingly, between the 16 and 32-cell stages, the proportion of injected and non-injected cells in the total, outside, and inside cell populations were comparable whether embryos had been injected with Lats2 and GFP or GFP mRNA alone (Figure 2F–H). In embryos injected with GFP mRNA alone, the proportion of injected and non-injected cells making up the total, outside, and inside cell populations remained constant throughout the time course. In contrast, starting around the 32-cell stage, the average proportion of Lats2-overexpressing cells making up the inside population began to increase dramatically.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F–H

claim: Lats2-overexpressing cells were equally likely to occupy inside position in the presence and absence of Sox2
source: However, we observed that Lats2-overexpressing cells were equally likely to occupy inside position in the presence and absence of Sox2 (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: LATS2 acts on cell positioning/survival independently of Sox2
source: Furthermore, Lats2-overexpressing cells were equally unlikely to occupy outside position in the presence and absence of Sox2 (Figure 3D). Therefore, although Lats2 overexpression is sufficient to induce expression of Sox2, LATS2 acts on cell positioning/survival independently of Sox2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Most Lats2-overexpressing outside cells lacked detectable aPKCz and PARD6B
source: At this stage, apical membrane components PARD6B and aPKCz were detected at the apical membrane of non-injected outside cells and outside cells injected with GFP only (Figure 4A–D). By contrast, most Lats2-overexpressing outside cells lacked detectable aPKCz and PARD6B (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A–D

claim: LATS2 is sufficient to antagonize localization of key apical domain proteins in outside cells
source: Therefore, LATS2 is sufficient to antagonize localization of key apical domain proteins in outside cells, providing a compelling mechanism for the observed repositioning of Lats2-overexpressing outside cells.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing loss of aPKCz and PARD6B in Lats2-overexpressing cells

claim: CDH1 was restricted to the basolateral membrane in Lats2-overexpressing outside cells
source: For example, CDH1 was restricted to the basolateral membrane (Figure 4E), while filamentous Actin and phospho-ERM were restricted to the apical domain in outside cells of both Lats2-overexpressing and non-injected outside cells (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: With decreasing number of wild type zygotic alleles of Wwtr1 and Yap1, embryos exhibited worsening phenotypes
source: However, with decreasing number of wild type zygotic alleles of Wwtr1 and Yap1, we observed worsening phenotypes (Figure 5B–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B–F

claim: In the complete absence of Wwtr1 and Yap1, embryos exhibited a severe loss of CDX2 and expansion of SOX2 in outside cells
source: In the complete absence of Wwtr1 and Yap1, we observed a severe loss of CDX2 and expansion of SOX2 in outside cells (Figure 5D–F), phenocopying Lats2 overexpression.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D–F

claim: Regulation of Sox2 expression is more sensitive to Wwtr1 and Yap1 dosage than is Cdx2
source: However, in embryos of intermediate genotypes, we observed expanded SOX2 and persistent, yet lower, expression levels of CDX2 (Figure 5C,E–F). Thus, regulation of Sox2 expression is more sensitive to Wwtr1 and Yap1 dosage than is Cdx2.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, E–F

claim: Intermediate doses of Wwtr1 and Yap1 produce outside cells expressing markers of mixed cell lineage at E3.25
source: Moreover, these observations indicate that intermediate doses of Wwtr1 and Yap1 produce outside cells expressing markers of mixed cell lineage at E3.25.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing coexpression of SOX2 and CDX2 in intermediate genotypes

claim: Embryos with one or fewer wild type alleles of Wwtr1 or Yap1 exhibited an increase in the number of inside cells and a reduction in the number of outside cells
source: Indeed, we observed skewed lineage contributions, correlating with the dosage of Wwtr1 and Yap1 (Figure 6A–D). Embryos with one or fewer wild type alleles of Wwtr1 or Yap1 exhibited an increase in the number of inside cells and a reduction in the number of outside cells (Figure 6A–B), consistent with altered cell positioning.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A–D

claim: The fewer outside cells in embryos lacking Wwtr1 and Yap1 exhibited ectopic expression of SOX2
source: Critically, the fewer outside cells in embryos lacking Wwtr1 and Yap1, which appeared stretched over the mass of inside cells, exhibited ectopic expression of SOX2 (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E–F

claim: WWTR1/YAP1 repress inner cell mass fate, downstream of LATS kinases
source: Therefore, WWTR1/YAP1 repress inner cell mass fate, downstream of LATS kinases.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing ectopic SOX2 and increased inside cells in Wwtr1/Yap1 mutants

claim: WWTR1 is a more potent repressor of Sox2 at E3.75 than YAP1
source: Intriguingly, our data also indicate that WWTR1 is a more potent repressor of Sox2 at E3.75 than YAP1 since embryos with a single wild type allele of Wwtr1 had significantly fewer cells expressing ectopic SOX2 then embryos with a single wild type allele of Yap1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,G

claim: Embryos with one or fewer doses of Wwtr1 or Yap1 showed greatly reduced aPKC at the apical membrane of outside cells
source: As expected, observed greatly reduced aPKC at the apical membrane of outside cells in embryos with one or fewer doses of Wwtr1 or Yap1 (Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: CDH1 and pERM were correctly localized in outside cells of mutant embryos at E3.75
source: Notably, however, other markers of apicobasal polarity, such as CDH1 and pERM were correctly localized in outside cells of mutant embryos at this stage (Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E), consistent with some normal cell polarization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E

claim: WWTR1 and YAP1 play a crucial role in the formation of the apical domain and maintaining the positioning and survival of outside cells while repressing expression of Sox2
source: Our observations indicate that WWTR1 and YAP1 play a crucial role in the formation of the apical domain and maintaining the positioning and survival of outside cells while repressing expression of Sox2.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental observations

claim: SOX2 is never detected in outside cells
source: Similarly, CDX2 is detected in inner cell mass, as well as trophectoderm, until blastocyst stages (McDole and Zheng, 2012; Ralston and Rossant, 2008; Strumpf et al., 2005). In striking contrast to these genes, SOX2 is never detected in outside cells (Wicklow et al., 2014), indicating that robust mechanisms must exist to minimize noise and prevent its aberrant expression in trophectoderm.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wicklow et al., 2014

claim: YAP1/WWTR1 are key components that repress Sox2 expression in outside cells of the embryo
source: Here, we identify YAP1/WWTR1 as key components that repress Sox2 expression in outside cells of the embryo.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claim: Manipulations known to antagonize YAP1/WWTR1 activity lead to ectopic expression of SOX2 in outside cells
source: Notably, manipulations known to antagonize YAP1/WWTR1 activity, including chemical inhibition of ROCK and overexpression of LATS2, lead to ectopic expression of SOX2 in outside cells, reinforcing the notion that YAP1/WWTR1 activity are crucial for repression of Sox2 in outside cells.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claim: Sox2 expression is more sensitive than Cdx2 to YAP1/WWTR1 activity
source: Additionally, we find that Sox2 expression is more sensitive than is Cdx2 to YAP1/WWTR1 activity, since intermediate doses of active YAP1/WWTR1 yield cells that coexpress both SOX2 and CDX2 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Inside cells could initially possess intermediate doses of active YAP1/WWTR1 at early blastocyst stages
source: This observation is consistent with the fact that CDX2 is initially detected in inside cells of the embryo during blastocyst formation (Dietrich and Hiiragi, 2007; McDole and Zheng, 2012; Ralston and Rossant, 2008), where SOX2 is also expressed (Wicklow et al., 2014). Thus, inside cells could initially possess intermediate doses of active YAP1/WWTR1 at this early stage.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and cited literature

claim: The HIPPO pathway ensures robust developmental transitions by rapidly nudging SOX2-expressing cells into their correct and final positions inside the embryo
source: In this way, the HIPPO pathway ensures robust developmental transitions, by rapidly nudging SOX2-expressing cells into their correct and final positions inside the embryo (Figure 7B).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: The timing of HIPPO-induced cell internalization coincides with loss of cell fate plasticity around the 32-cell stage
source: Consistent with our proposed model, the timing of HIPPO-induced cell internalization coincides with loss of cell fate plasticity around the 32-cell stage (Posfai et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Posfai et al., 2017

claim: The timing of HIPPO-induced cell internalization coincides with the formation of mature tight junctions among outside cells
source: This timing also coincides with the formation of mature tight junctions among outside cells (Sheth et al., 1997), which reinforce and intensify differences in HIPPO signaling activity between inside and outside compartments of the embryo (Hirate and Sasaki, 2014; Leung and Zernicka-Goetz, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sheth et al., 1997, Hirate and Sasaki, 2014, and Leung and Zernicka-Goetz, 2013

claim: HIPPO signaling can interfere with trophectoderm epithelialization
source: Our observations indicate that HIPPO signaling can, in turn, interfere with trophectoderm epithelialization.
evidence: Based on experimental observations of tight junction and apical domain defects

claim: HIPPO engages in a negative feedback loop with cell polarity components
source: Therefore, we propose that HIPPO engages in a negative feedback loop with cell polarity components (Figure 7B).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: A small proportion of conflicted cells undergo cell death downstream of YAP1/WWTR1
source: We propose two mechanisms by which HIPPO signaling eliminates cells from the trophectoderm, both of which are downstream of YAP1/WWTR1 (Figure 7C). First, a small proportion of conflicted cells undergo cell death.
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 7C and TUNEL assays

claim: Cell lethality due to elevated HIPPO can be rescued by increasing levels of nuclear YAP1
source: We showed that cell lethality due to elevated HIPPO can be rescued by increasing levels of nuclear YAP1, suggesting that YAP1 activity normally provides a pro-survival signal to trophectoderm cells, consistent with the proposed role of YAP1 in promoting proliferation in non-eutherian mammals (Frankenberg, 2018).
evidence: Based on experimental data and citation to Frankenberg, 2018

claim: Deletion of Sox2 did not rescue survival of outside cells in which HIPPO signaling was artificially elevated
source: Moreover, deletion of Sox2 did not rescue survival of outside cells in which HIPPO signaling was artificially elevated, arguing that HIPPO resolves cell fate conflicts independently of lineage-specific genes.
evidence: Based on experimental data from Sox2 deletion experiments

claim: Cells with elevated HIPPO signaling drive their own internalization
source: The second way that conflicted cells are eliminated from the trophectoderm is that cells with elevated HIPPO signaling drive their own internalization.
evidence: Based on experimental observations of cell repositioning

claim: Cells in which Tead4 has been knocked down become internalized
source: This is consistent with the observation that cells in which Tead4 has been knocked down become internalized (Mihajlović et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mihajlović et al., 2015

claim: Tead4 loss of function preserves the apical domain in outside cells
source: However, in contrast to Tead4 loss of function, which preserves the apical domain in outside cells (Mihajlović et al., 2015; Nishioka et al., 2008), we observed that Yap1/Wwtr1 loss of function leads loss of apical PARD6D/aPKC.
evidence: Supported by citations to Mihajlović et al., 2015 and Nishioka et al., 2008

claim: YAP1/WWTR1 could partner with proteins other than TEAD4 to regulate apical domain formation
source: These observations suggest that YAP1/WWTR1 could partner with proteins other than TEAD4 to regulate apical domain formation.
evidence: Inferred from differences between Tead4 and Yap1/Wwtr1 loss of function phenotypes

claim: TEAD1 has been proposed to play an essential role in the early embryo
source: Consistent with this proposal, TEAD1 has been proposed to play an essential role in the early embryo (Sasaki, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sasaki, 2017

claim: PARD6B/aPKC are essential for outside cell positioning
source: Nevertheless, since PARD6B/aPKC are essential for outside cell positioning (Dard et al., 2009; Hirate et al., 2015; Plusa et al., 2005), the loss of the apical domain could affect cell positioning in several ways.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dard et al., 2009, Hirate et al., 2015, and Plusa et al., 2005

claim: Loss of PARD6B/aPKC would eventually lead to cell depolarization
source: For instance, loss of PARD6B/aPKC would eventually lead to cell depolarization (Alarcon, 2010), which could influence any of the processes normally governing the allocation of inside cells, such as oriented cleavage, cell contractility, or apical constriction (Korotkevich et al., 2017; Maître et al., 2016; Samarage et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alarcon, 2010, Korotkevich et al., 2017, Maître et al., 2016, and Samarage et al., 2015

claim: SOX2 does not play a role in cell positioning
source: Our studies also revealed that SOX2 does not play a role in cell positioning.
evidence: Based on experimental data from Sox2 deletion experiments

claim: SOX2 dwells longer in select nuclei of four-cell stage embryos that are destined to contribute to the inner cell mass
source: This observation sheds light on a recent study, which showed that SOX2 dwells longer in select nuclei of four-cell stage embryos that are destined to contribute to the inner cell mass (White et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 2016

claim: SOX2 is associated with future pluripotent state but does not alone contribute to all aspects of pluripotency, such as inside positioning
source: We propose that SOX2 is associated with future pluripotent state but does not alone contribute to all aspects of pluripotency, such as inside positioning.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing Sox2-independent cell positioning

claim: Maternal and zygotic YAP1 and WWTR1 repress Sox2 while promoting expression of the trophectoderm gene Cdx2 in parallel
source: Here, we unveil novel roles for the HIPPO signaling pathway in controlling cell positioning and expression of Sox2, the first marker of pluripotency in the mouse early embryo. We show that maternal and zygotic YAP1 and WWTR1 repress Sox2 while promoting expression of the trophectoderm gene Cdx2 in parallel.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claim: Sox2 is more sensitive than Cdx2 to Yap1/Wwtr1 dosage, leading cells to a state of conflicted cell fate when YAP1/WWTR1 activity is moderate
source: Yet, Sox2 is more sensitive than Cdx2 to Yap1/Wwtr1 dosage, leading cells to a state of conflicted cell fate when YAP1/WWTR1 activity is moderate.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claim: HIPPO signaling activity resolves conflicted cell fate by repositioning cells to the interior of the embryo, independent of its role in regulating Sox2 expression
source: Remarkably, HIPPO signaling activity resolves conflicted cell fate by repositioning cells to the interior of the embryo, independent of its role in regulating Sox2 expression.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claim: HIPPO antagonizes apical localization of Par complex components PARD6B and aPKC
source: Rather, HIPPO antagonizes apical localization of Par complex components PARD6B and aPKC.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claim: Negative feedback between HIPPO and Par complex components ensure robust lineage segregation
source: Thus, negative feedback between HIPPO and Par complex components ensure robust lineage segregation.

claim: Progenitors of inner cell mass are first morphologically apparent at the 16 cell stage as unpolarized cells residing inside the morula
source: Progenitors of inner cell mass are first morphologically apparent at the 16 cell stage as unpolarized cells residing inside the morula (reviewed in Frum and Ralston, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frum and Ralston, 2017

claim: At the 16 cell stage, pluripotency genes such as Pou5f1 (Oct4) and Nanog do not specifically label inside cells
source: However, at this stage, pluripotency genes such as Pou5f1 (Oct4) and Nanog, do not specifically label inside cells (Dietrich and Hiiragi, 2007; Niwa et al., 2005; Palmieri et al., 1994; Strumpf et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dietrich and Hiiragi, 2007, Niwa et al., 2005, Palmieri et al., 1994, and Strumpf et al., 2005

claim: CDX2 is essential for trophectoderm development
source: Thus, the first cell fate decision has been studied mainly from the perspective of trophectoderm specification because the transcription factor CDX2, which is essential for trophectoderm development (Strumpf et al., 2005), is expressed specifically in outer cells of the 16 cell embryo (Ralston and Rossant, 2008), and has provided a way to distinguish future trophectoderm cells from non-trophectoderm cells.

source: Knowledge of CDX2 as a marker of trophectoderm cell fate enabled the discovery of mechanisms that sense cellular differences in polarity and position in the embryo, and then respond by regulating expression of Cdx2 (Nishioka et al., 2009).

source: We previously showed that Sox2 is restricted to inside cells by a Cdx2-independent mechanism (Wicklow et al., 2014), which differs from Oct4 and Nanog, which are restricted to the inner cell mass by CDX2 (Niwa et al., 2005; Strumpf et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Niwa et al., 2005 and Strumpf et al., 2005

claim: Sox2 and Cdx2 are regulated in parallel, leading to complementary inside/outside expression patterns
source: Thus, Sox2 and Cdx2 are regulated in parallel, leading to complementary inside/outside expression patterns.

source: Additionally, quantitative RT-PCR showed that Sox2 mRNA levels are elevated in ROCKi-treated embryos (Kono et al., 2014), suggesting that ROCK1/2 activity leads to transcriptional repression of Sox2.

source: Among these is YAP1, a transcriptional partner of TEAD4 (Nishioka et al., 2009), since ROCK activity is required for the nuclear localization of YAP1 (Kono et al., 2014).

claim: Substitution of alanine at serine 112 leads YAP1 to be constitutively nuclear and constitutively active
source: Substitution of alanine at serine 112 leads YAP1 to be constitutively nuclear and constitutively active (YAP1CA hereafter) (Dong et al., 2007; Nishioka et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2007).

source: To functionally test of the role of YAP1 in repressing expression of Sox2, we injected one of two blastomeres with mRNA encoding LATS2 kinase, which inactivates YAP1 and, presumably, the related protein WWTR1 by phosphorylation, causing their cytoplasmic retention (Nishioka et al., 2008).

claim: Yap1 null embryos survive until E9.0
source: Yap1 null embryos survive until E9.0 (Morin-Kensicki et al., 2006), suggesting that oocyte-expressed (maternal) Yap1 (Yu et al., 2016), or the Yap1 paralogue Wwtr1 (Varelas et al., 2010) are important for preimplantation development.

source: For example, Oct4 and Nanog are expressed in both inner cell mass and trophectoderm until after blastocyst formation (Dietrich and Hiiragi, 2007; Strumpf et al., 2005).

source: Similarly, CDX2 is detected in inner cell mass, as well as trophectoderm, until blastocyst stages (McDole and Zheng, 2012; Ralston and Rossant, 2008; Strumpf et al., 2005).

source: This observation is consistent with the fact that CDX2 is initially detected in inside cells of the embryo during blastocyst formation (Dietrich and Hiiragi, 2007; McDole and Zheng, 2012; Ralston and Rossant, 2008), where SOX2 is also expressed (Wicklow et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dietrich and Hiiragi, 2007, McDole and Zheng, 2012, and Ralston and Rossant, 2008

claim: Outside cells have greatly reduced YAP1/WWTR1 activity, owing to elevated LATS activity
source: By contrast, outside cells have greatly reduced YAP1/WWTR1 activity, owing to elevated LATS activity.

source: This is in line with the observed increase in the level of apoptosis detected after the 32-cell stage (Copp, 1978).

source: We showed that cell lethality due to elevated HIPPO can be rescued by increasing levels of nuclear YAP1, suggesting that YAP1 activity normally provides a pro-survival signal to trophectoderm cells, consistent with the proposed role of YAP1 in promoting proliferation in non-eutherian mammals (Frankenberg, 2018).

claim: SOX2 activity has been proposed to bias inner cell mass fate
source: In support of this hypothesis, SOX2 activity has been proposed to bias inner cell mass fate (Goolam et al., 2016; White et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goolam et al., 2016 and White et al., 2016

claim: Trophectoderm cell fate has been proposed to be determined by apically localized membrane components that maintain the position of future trophectoderm cells on the embryo surface
source: Trophectoderm cell fate has been proposed to be determined by apically localized membrane components that maintain the position of future trophectoderm cells on the embryo surface (Anani et al., 2014; Korotkevich et al., 2017; Maître et al., 2016; Maître et al., 2015; Samarage et al., 2015; Zenker et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Anani et al., 2014, Korotkevich et al., 2017, Maître et al., 2016, Maître et al., 2015, Samarage et al., 2015, and Zenker et al., 2018

claim: The apical membrane components aPKC and PARD6B are required for maintaining outside cell position and trophectoderm fate
source: For example, the apical membrane components aPKC and PARD6B are required for maintaining outside cell position and trophectoderm fate (Alarcon, 2010; Dard et al., 2009; Hirate et al., 2015; Plusa et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alarcon, 2010, Dard et al., 2009, Hirate et al., 2015, and Plusa et al., 2005

claim: Lats2-overexpressing outside cells initially possess hallmarks of apicobasal polarization, but aPKC and PARD6B fail to properly localize, leading to the eventual depolarization and internalization of outside cells
source: Thus, we propose that Lats2-overexpressing outside cells initially possess hallmarks of apicobasal polarization, but aPKC and PARD6B fail to properly localize, leading to the eventual depolarization and internalization of outside cells.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations of polarity markers

claim: Embryos were collected at E2.5 and treated with ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (ROCKi) or DMSO (control) for 24 hr
source: (A) Experimental design: embryos were collected at E2.5 and treated with ROCK inhibitor Y-27632 (ROCKi) or DMSO (control) for 24 hr.
evidence: Experimental design described in Figure 1A

claim: PARD6B and CDH1 are mislocalized to the entire cell membrane of all cells in ROCKi-treated embryos
source: (B–B') Confocal images of apical (PARD6B) and basolateral (CDH1) membrane components in control and ROCKi-treated embryos. As expected, PARD6B and CDH1 are mislocalized to the entire cell membrane of all cells in ROCKi-treated embryos, demonstrating effective ROCK inhibition (n = number of embryos examined).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1B-B'

claim: In control embryos, SOX2 is detected only in inside cells, while in ROCKi-treated embryos, SOX2 is detected in inside and outside cells
source: (C–C') In control embryos, SOX2 is detected only in inside cells, while in ROCKi-treated embryos, SOX2 is detected in inside and outside cells (arrowheads, outside cells; n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1C-C'

claim: YAP1CA was injected into one of two blastomeres at the 2 cell stage and evaluated 48 hr later
source: (B) YAP1CA was injected into one of two blastomeres at the 2 cell stage and evaluated 48 hr later.
evidence: Experimental design described in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: In non-injected cells, YAP1 is exclusively nuclear in outside cells while pYAP1 is exclusively cytoplasmic in inside cells
source: (C) In non-injected cells, YAP1 is exclusively nuclear in outside cells while pYAP1 is exclusively cytoplasmic in inside cells. By contrast, YAP1 is detected in the nucleus of Yap1CA-injected cells, regardless of their position, demonstrating that YAP1CA is constitutively nuclear.
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Yap1CA can still be phosphorylated on non-mutated residues, but this is not sufficient to alter YAP1 nuclear localization
source: Additionally, analysis of pYAP1 in YAP1CA-injected cells shows that Yap1CA can still be phosphorylated on non-mutated residues, but this is not sufficient to alter YAP1 nuclear localization (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Cells injected with Lats2 and GFP contributed almost exclusively to the inner cell mass, leaving only cellular fragments in the trophectoderm
source: (B) Cells injected with GFP (dotted line) contributed to trophectoderm and inner cell mass, while cells injected with Lats2 and GFP (dotted line) contributed almost exclusively to the inner cell mass, leaving only cellular fragments in the trophectoderm (arrows), suggestive of cell death (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Cells injected with GFP/Lats2 were overrepresented within the inside cell population and underrepresented in the outside and total cell populations, relative to cells injected with GFP alone
source: (C) Proportion of inside, outside, and total cell populations across multiple embryos, which were comprised of non-injected cells, or cells injected with either GFP or GFP/Lats2 mRNAs. Cells injected with GFP/Lats2 were overrepresented within the inside cell population and underrepresented in the outside and total cell populations, relative to cells injected with GFP alone (P, chi-squared test).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The average number of outside cells is reduced in embryos injected with Lats2/GFP, relative to GFP-injected
source: (E) Average number of outside and total cells per embryo. The average number of outside cells is reduced in embryos injected with Lats2/GFP, relative to GFP-injected (p, student's t-test).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Injection with Lats2/GFP increases the overall number of inside cells compared to injection with GFP only through increasing the number of injected cells contributing to the inside cell population
source: (I) Contribution of injected and non-injected cells to the inside cell population, following injection with GFP or Lats2/GFP. Injection with Lats2/GFP increases the overall number of inside cells compared to injection with GFP only through increasing the number of injected cells contributing to the inside cell population, without affecting the number of non-injected cells contributing to the inside cell population (p, student's t-test).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2I

claim: Embryo injected with Lats2 and GFP mRNA shows elevated TUNEL-positive foci in the outside cells
source: (B) Embryo injected in one of two cells with Lats2 and GFP mRNA and then cultured until the blastocyst stage shows elevated TUNEL-positive foci in the outside cells (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Embryo injected with Yap1CA, Lats2 and GFP mRNA shows reduced TUNEL-positive foci in the outside cells
source: (C) Embryo injected in one of two cells with Yap1CA, Lats2 and GFP mRNA and then cultured until the blastocyst stage shows reduced TUNEL-positive foci in the outside cells (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Yap1CA-overexpression partially reverses the effect of Lats2-overexpression on cellular localization to the inside of the embryo
source: (B) Contribution of injected cells to inside and outside embryo compartments. Yap1CA-overexpression partially reverses the effect of Lats2-overexpression on cellular localization to the inside of the embryo (P, chi-squared test).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Yap1CA-cooverexpression reduces the proportion of Lats2-overexpressing cells observed in the inside population
source: (C) Proportion of non-injected cells and injected cells contributing to the inside population in embryos injected with the indicated mRNAs. Yap1CA-cooverexpression reduces the proportion of Lats2-overexpressing cells observed in the inside population (P, chi-squared test, n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: Yap1CA-cooverexpression increases the proportion of Lats2-overexpressing cells observed in the outside population
source: (D) Proportion of non-injected cells and injected cells contributing to the outside population in embryos injected with the indicated mRNAs. Yap1CA-cooverexpression increases the proportion of Lats2-overexpressing cells observed in the outside population (P, chi-squared test, n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D

claim: Lats2/GFP-overexpressing cells contribute almost exclusively to the inner cell mass in the presence or absence of Sox2
source: (B) Lats2/GFP-overexpressing cells (dotted line) contribute almost exclusively to the inner cell mass in the presence or absence of Sox2 (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Sox2 is dispensable for inside positioning by Lats2-overexpression
source: (C) Proportion of non-injected cells and cells injected with Lats2/GFP mRNAs contributing to inner cell mass in the indicated genetic backgrounds. No significant differences were observed based on embryo genotype, indicating that Sox2 is dispensable for inside positioning by Lats2-overexpression (P, chi-squared test; n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: At 16–32 cell stages, aPKCz is detectable in GFP-overexpressing and in non-injected cells, but not in Lats2-overexpressing cells
source: (B) At 16–32 cell stages, aPKCz is detectable in GFP-overexpressing and in non-injected cells, but not in Lats2-overexpressing cells (arrowheads, n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: At 16–32 cell stages, CDH1 is localized to the basolateral membrane in both Lats2-overexpressing and non-injected cells
source: (E) At 16–32 cell stages, CDH1 is localized to the basolateral membrane in both Lats2-overexpressing and non-injected cells (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: At 16–32 cell stages, filamentous Actin is apically enriched in Lats2-overexpressing and non-injected cells
source: (F) At 16–32 cell stages, Phalloidin staining demonstrates that filamentous Actin is apically enriched in Lats2-overexpressing and non-injected cells (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: At 16–32 cell stages, pERM is localized to the apical membrane in both Lats2-overexpressing and non-injected cells
source: (G) At 16–32 cell stages, pERM is localized to the apical membrane in both Lats2-overexpressing and non-injected cells (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 4G

claim: CDX2 staining is more intense in outside cells than inside cells and SOX2 staining is specific to inside cells in wild type embryos at E3.25
source: (A) CDX2 and SOX2 in wild type embryos at E3.25 (16–32 cell stages). CDX2 staining is more intense in outside cells than inside cells and SOX2 staining is specific to inside cells (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1 and heterozygous for Wwtr1 and Yap1 exhibit normal CDX2 and SOX2 expression
source: (B) Embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1 with and heterozygous for Wwtr1 and Yap1 (which we consider to have 2 doses of WWTR1/YAP1) exhibit normal CDX2 and SOX2 expression (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1 and heterozygous for either Wwtr1 or Yap1 exhibit a high degree of ectopic SOX2 in outside cells but continue to express CDX2
source: (C) Embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1 and heterozygous for either Wwtr1 or Yap1 (1 dose of WWTR1/YAP1) exhibit a high degree of ectopic SOX2 in outside cells (arrowheads), but continue to express CDX2, although the levels appear reduced (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Embryos lacking maternal and zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 have the most severe phenotype, with a high degree of ectopic SOX2 in outside cells and little or no detectable CDX2
source: (D) Embryos lacking maternal and zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 (0 doses of WWTR1/YAP1) have the most severe phenotype, with a high degree of ectopic SOX2 in outside cells (arrowheads) and little or no detectable CDX2 (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: The number of inside cells increases as the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 alleles is reduced
source: The number of inside cells increases as the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 alleles is reduced (p, student's t-test, n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The number of outside cells decreases as the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 alleles is reduced
source: (B) Quantification of the average number of outside cells per embryo with decreasing dose of Wwtr1 and Yap1. The number of outside cells decreases as the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 alleles is reduced (p, student's t-test, n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The number of total cells decreases as the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 is reduced
source: (C) Quantification of the average number of total cells per embryos with decreasing dose of wild type zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1. The number of total cells decreases as the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 is reduced (p, student's t-test, n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: The ratio of inside to outside cells increases as the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 is reduced
source: (D) Quantification of the average ratio of inside to outside cells per embryo with decreasing dose of Wwtr1 and Yap1. The ratio of inside to outside cells increases as the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 is reduced (p, student's t-test, n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: E3.75 embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1 and heterozygous for zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 cavitate and repress Sox2 in outside cells
source: (E') E3.75 embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1 and heterozygous for zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 cavitate and repress Sox2 in outside cells, leading to inner cell mass-specific expression of SOX2 similar to wild type embryos (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6E'

claim: Embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1 but with only one wild type allele of Wwtr1 or Yap1 fail to cavitate and repress Sox2 in outside cells
source: (E'') Embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1 but with only one wild type allele of Wwtr1 or Yap1 fail to cavitate and repress Sox2 in outside cells, leading to ectopic SOX2 in outside cells (arrowheads, n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6E''

claim: Embryos lacking maternal and zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 fail to cavitate and repress Sox2 in outside cells
source: (E''') Embryos lacking maternal and zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 fail to cavitate and repress Sox2 in outside cells, leading to ectopic SOX2 in outside cells (arrowheads, n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6E'''

claim: The percentage of outside cells with ectopic SOX2 increases as the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 alleles is reduced
source: (F) Quantification of ectopic SOX2 detected in embryos such as those shown in panels E-E'''. The percentage of outside cells with ectopic SOX2 increases as the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 alleles is reduced (p, student's t-test, n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Extensive TUNEL staining is observed in embryos lacking maternal and zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 indicative of cell death
source: (G) TUNEL analysis of embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1 heterozygous for zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 or lacking maternal and zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1. Extensive TUNEL staining is observed in embryos lacking maternal and zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 indicative of cell death. Max projections of all confocal sections from a single embryo are shown (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6G

claim: aPKC is not localized to the apical membrane of embryos with no zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1
source: (H) aPKCz staining in embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1, either heterozygous for zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 or with no zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1. aPKC is not localized to the apical membrane of embryos with no zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6H

claim: ZO-1 is disorganized in embryos with no zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1, suggesting that formation of a mature epithelium depends on Wwtr1 and Yap1
source: (I) ZO-1 staining in embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1, either heterozygous for zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 or with no zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1. ZO-1 is disorganized in embryos with no zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1, suggesting that formation of a mature epithelium depends on Wwtr1 and Yap1 (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6I

claim: pERM is localized to apical membranes and CDH1 to basolateral membranes regardless of the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 alleles
source: (J) pERM and CDH1 staining in embryos lacking maternal Wwtr1 and Yap1, either heterozygous for zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1 or with no zygotic Wwtr1 and Yap1. pERM is localized to apical membranes and CDH1 to basolateral membranes regardless of the dose of wild type Wwtr1 and Yap1 alleles (n = embryos).
evidence: Experimental data shown in Figure 6J
